title: Who's at This Address?
summary: Forkful's services keep moving as they autoscale. How does one service find another — and how do the apps find any of them?

goals.text: See why hard-coded addresses break once instances move
Compare client-side, server-side and DNS discovery
Keep traffic off sick instances with health checks
Put an API gateway in front as the single front door

steps.title: Payments lives at 10.0.3.17
body: Forkful takes food orders. At checkout, the Orders service calls the Payments service — and finds it the simplest way possible: Payments' IP address sits in a config file.
With one long-lived Payments server, that works. Nothing moves, so nothing needs finding.

steps.title: The address went stale
body: Payments moves to containers with autoscaling. On Friday evening it scales to three instances — and every deploy or scale event hands out fresh IP addresses. The old server at 10.0.3.17 was replaced an hour ago.

Orders is still calling the address in its config. Every charge goes to a machine that no longer exists, times out, and the checkout fails. In a dynamic fleet, where a service lives is runtime data, not configuration.

callout.text: Containers, autoscaling and rolling deploys all change addresses — often many times a day.

changes: + Payments autoscaled to 3 instances with new IPs
~ Orders still calls the old address

steps.title: A phone book for services
body: A service registry keeps a live list of instances per service. Each Payments instance registers its address when it starts and sends a heartbeat every few seconds; if heartbeats stop, the registry drops it.
Now Orders asks by name — "where is payments?" — and gets the current list of healthy addresses. Consul, etcd/ZooKeeper-backed registries and Kubernetes' own endpoint lists all play this role.
changes: ~ Orders looks Payments up by name

steps.title: The caller picks an instance
body: In client-side discovery, Orders fetches the instance list, caches it, and load-balances across it itself. No extra hop, and the client can be smart — prefer the same zone, retry on another instance.

The catch is staleness. When an instance crashes, the registry notices after a few missed heartbeats, but Orders keeps using its cached list until the next refresh. For those seconds, some calls still go to a dead address — so clients also need timeouts and retries. Every language your services use needs this logic too.
changes: ~ Orders caches the instance list and balances itself
~ One instance crashes; the registry evicts it

steps.title: One stable name in front
body: With server-side discovery, Orders calls a single stable name — payments.internal — and a load balancer behind that name watches the registry and spreads calls over healthy instances.
Callers stay simple and language-agnostic, and the balancer updates the moment the registry changes. The cost is one more network hop and one more component that must itself be highly available.

steps.title: Discovery through DNS
body: The most universal option is DNS-based discovery: the registry publishes records, and payments.svc resolves to the current instance IPs. Every language and tool already speaks DNS.

But DNS answers are cached — by resolvers, by the OS, sometimes by the runtime for far longer than the record's TTL. After an instance dies, some callers keep its address until their cache expires. Keep TTLs short and still expect a few failed calls to retry.

callout.text: Kubernetes Services combine both ideas: a DNS name that points at a stable virtual IP, which the cluster balances over ready pods.

changes: + DNS records published from the registry
~ Orders resolves payments.svc, cached for 30 s
~ One instance died; cached answers still include it

steps.title: Only send traffic to the ready
body: Being registered isn't the same as being able to serve. Health checks come in two kinds: a liveness check asks "is the process stuck?" (if so, restart it), and a readiness check asks "can you take traffic right now?"
A fresh instance warming its cache answers /ready with 503, so it stays out of rotation until it's actually useful. Instances that start failing readiness are pulled out before callers notice.

steps.title: One front door for the apps
body: Inside the network, services can find each other. But the phone app shouldn't know about Menu, Orders and Payments, their addresses, or how they're split — that would freeze the internal design into every installed app.

An API gateway is the single public entry point. It terminates TLS, checks the caller's token, applies rate limits, and routes /menu and /orders to the right service using the same discovery underneath.
changes: + Menu, Orders and Payments behind it

steps.title: Keep the front door thin
body: Shared concerns belong at the gateway: a scraper with no token is turned away with 401, a flood gets 429, and services never see either.

But every request now passes through it, so run several stateless copies, and resist putting business logic there. A gateway that knows about discounts and order rules becomes a new monolith that every team has to change and deploy.

callout.text: If the gateway is down, everything is down. Treat it like the most critical service you run.

changes: + Scraper bot rejected at the gateway

steps.title: Who's at this address: recap
body:
• Registry → instances register and heartbeat; callers look up by name
  • Client-side → no extra hop, but caches go stale and logic lives in every client
  • Server-side / DNS → simple callers; one more hop, or TTL-cached answers
  • Health checks → readiness keeps traffic off instances that can't serve
  • API gateway → one thin, replicated front door for auth, limits and routing
